notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 46, based only on the pages I could read. Bible Hub's verse pages show excerpts from several commentaries, but some excerpts don't name their author. Where that happens, I say "an unnamed commentator on Bible Hub" instead of guessing.

**One thing to know first:** I didn't find any source that splits these verses along denominational lines (Baptist versus Methodist, and so on). The real divide is between two ways of reading the whole temple vision:
- **A literal future temple:** these chapters describe a real temple in a coming 1,000-year reign of Christ on earth (the "millennium"). This view is called premillennial or dispensational.
- **A symbolic temple:** the chapters are a picture fulfilled in Christ and the church.

I've flagged this divide at the verses where it matters.

---

**Overview**
- Ellicott says verses 1–15 really belong with chapter 45. Because the prince must provide the sacrifices for himself and the people (45:17), these verses explain how he behaves at them. He must always be present, while the people only have to attend at the yearly festivals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary sees three parts: extra rules for the prince and people at worship (vv. 1–15), how the prince may hand on his land (vv. 16–18), and the sacrificial kitchens (vv. 19–24). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html
- **Literal view:** Guzik (Enduring Word) says these descriptions should be taken literally, not merely spiritualized. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/

**v. 1**
- Ellicott: 44:1–3 already said the outer east gate stays shut except for the prince. The same rule now covers the inner east gate, and the days it opens for him are named: Sabbaths and New Moons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Guzik quotes Feinberg: the stress on Sabbath and New Moon "should indicate the Jewish setting of the passage", not Christian ground. He also notes that Israel's calendar followed the moon, so the New Moon mattered to them in a way it doesn't to us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/
- Guzik also quotes the older writer Trapp, who applies the verse to Christians: under the gospel we have clearer light and free access, especially on Lord's days. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/
- **Symbolic reading:** an unnamed commentator on Bible Hub reads the inner court gate "in the mystical sense" as the ministry of the Gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/46-1.htm
- Textual note: Ewald followed the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) and changed the text to read the *outer* court gate. The Pulpit Commentary disagrees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/46-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: the prince comes in through the outer east gate, crosses to the inner gate and worships at its threshold while the priests prepare his sacrifices. He doesn't enter the inner court or take on any priestly role. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Guzik quotes Block: standing at the gatepost lets the prince, as guardian and patron of worship, watch the priests at work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: the people don't worship where the prince does. They stay in the outer court, at the entrance of the inner east gate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Another commentator on Bible Hub sums up the difference: the prince came in by the outer east gate, while the people came only through the outer north and south gates and went no further than the front of the middle gate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/46-1.htm
- Pulpit Commentary (sermon notes): we cannot grant to any priest a power of attorney to execute our religious contracts in our stead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html

**vv. 4–5**
- Ellicott: the law of Moses required two lambs on the Sabbath (Numbers 28:9). Here that is greatly increased, the grain offering with the ram is larger, and the amount with the lambs is left to the prince's generosity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Pulpit Commentary on "as much as he is able": literally a gift of his hand, meaning not a handful but whatever his hand can reach. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html
- Matthew Henry: God considers what we are able to give, but this gives no cover to people who pretend they can't afford it, or who waste their means on other things. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_046.cfm
- Feinberg, quoted by Guzik, criticizes those who insist on keeping a seventh-day Sabbath today. He says the Sabbath also included set sacrifices by an authorized priest at a place God chose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/

**vv. 6–7**
- Ellicott: the law required two bulls, seven lambs and a ram for the New Moon, plus a goat as a sin offering. So this offering is smaller, and the goat isn't mentioned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Matthew Henry: those who do much for God regularly must still, on some occasions, do more. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/46-4.html

**v. 8**
- Pulpit Commentary: this verse starts the rules for worship at the appointed feasts by saying how the prince enters and leaves the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: all Israelite men had to attend the great feasts, so the crowds were huge. The rule keeps order: whichever outer gate you enter by, north or south, you leave by the opposite one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Block, quoted by Guzik, says the crowds would otherwise have been a logistical nightmare. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/
- Spiritual readings:
  - Pulpit Commentary (J.D. Davies): every visit to the sanctuary either helps or hinders a person's spiritual life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html
  - Biblical Illustrator: we should go on to the opposite good of what we already have. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-46.html
  - Bible Hub's chapter summary: worshippers leave changed. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/46.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: at the yearly feasts the people are there themselves, so the prince no longer needs to represent them. He worships among them and uses the same north and south gates. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Guzik sees servant leadership here. He quotes F.B. Meyer applying it to Jesus: "He never puts His sheep forth without going before them." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/
- Pulpit Commentary (sermon notes) reads it as "Christ is in the midst of his people." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the new grain-offering amounts from verses 5 and 7 and 45:24 are repeated for the feasts. The only different amount is for the daily sacrifice (v. 14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: he still comes in by the east gate, but this time the gate is shut as soon as he leaves, rather than staying open until evening. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Trapp, quoted by Guzik, saw in this verse "warrant for our week day lectures", i.e. weekday Bible teaching. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/
- A Bible Hub article suggests the freewill and peace offerings here may show that some of these sacrifices are joyful thanksgiving rather than atonement. https://biblehub.com/q/why_sacrifices_in_the_millennial_kingdom.htm

**vv. 13–15**
- Ellicott: the lamb is the same as in the law of Moses, but it is offered only in the morning, not morning and evening. The flour goes up from a tenth to a sixth of an ephah, and the oil from a quarter to a third of a hin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Why no evening offering? The Pulpit Commentary thinks the difference was deliberate, though it can't say why. Currey thought the evening offering may still have been intended. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html
  - Guzik quotes an older writer who also argues the evening sacrifice is included. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/
- Another commentator on Bible Hub: the daily sacrifice is the whole congregation's duty, supervised by the priests, not the prince's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/46-15.htm
- **Main debate (vv. 13–15): why sacrifices after Christ?**
  - *Literal view, sacrifices as memorials.* Guzik: daily offerings will memorialize Jesus' perfect sacrifice at the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/
  - GotQuestions: most premillennial scholars see the sacrifices as memorials, a reminder like the Lord's Supper. https://www.gotquestions.org/millennial-sacrifices.html
  - *Literal view, sacrifices for ceremonial cleansing.* Precept Austin cites Hullinger, who argues the sacrifices mainly remove ritual uncleanness and keep the temple from being defiled. It also notes Ezekiel calls them for "atonement," not a "memorial." The writer admits he isn't sure why they will be required. https://www.preceptaustin.org/the_millennium_3
  - *Disagreement inside this camp.* Precept Austin cites Walvoord: literal millennial sacrifices are a main point of objection for amillennialists (who don't expect a literal 1,000-year reign), and not all premillennialists hold them either. https://www.preceptaustin.org/the-millennium-in-the-old-and-new-testament
  - *Symbolic view.* Ellicott's note on 44:3 says the prince is the same person as "David" in 34:23–24, i.e. the Messiah. He calls this a conclusive reason for regarding the sacrificial worship of Ezekiel 46 as symbolical. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/44.htm
  - Ligonier: the temple's measurements look symbolic. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-sees-new-temple
  - The Gospel Coalition: the temple prophecies, including Ezekiel 40–48, are fulfilled and completed in Christ, the church and the new creation. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-temple/
  - Guzik reports a critic who says this symbolic view was "favored by the church Fathers and the Reformers." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/
  - An unnamed commentator on Bible Hub (v. 15) says the verse means all the Lord's people, who are all priests to God offering daily spiritual sacrifices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/46-15.htm
- Application, Pulpit Commentary: giving oneself to God is not a one-time act but a continuing habit of the soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: the prince's land (45:7–8) was big enough to remove any temptation to violence or extortion, and it had to stay in his family. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- **Who is the prince?** Opinions differ:
  - Guzik: because the prince has sons, and offers a sin offering in 45:22, it is unlikely that the prince is Jesus Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/
  - A Bible Commentary Knowledge note, cited on Precept Austin, makes the same kind of point and takes him to be a resurrected David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/the_millennium_3
  - Bible Hub's summary: probably a future descendant of David. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/46.htm
  - Ellicott, by contrast, takes the prince to be the Messiah (see vv. 13–15).

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: a gift of land to anyone outside his sons fell under the law of Leviticus 25 and went back in the Jubilee, here called "the year of liberty." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: this marks a clear difference between the privileges of sons and those of servants. It links this to Paul's contrast between the gospel and the Law. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html
- An unnamed commentator on Bible Hub reads the "servants" as unregenerate ministers of the word and nominal believers. Their gifts are temporary, while the sons are joint heirs with Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/46-17.htm

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: a fresh warning against the prince oppressing the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Another commentator on Bible Hub points to the story of Ahab and Naboth, 1 Kings 21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/46-18.htm
- Matthew Henry: rulers do better to win their people's affection by protecting their rights than to win their land by taking it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_046.cfm
- Guzik: Israel will have righteous leadership throughout the millennial period. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/
- An unnamed commentator on Bible Hub, reading symbolically: Christ, the Prince, will never take any part of his people's inheritance from them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/46-18.htm

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: the people could eat only the peace offerings, but the priests also had to eat the sin and guilt offerings and most of the grain offerings. He takes the "place" to mean two places, one at the west end of each block of priests' rooms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: the law required the meat of every sacrifice except the Passover to be boiled, and the grain offering, if not already cooked, to be baked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the phrase about not passing holiness to the people is usually read in the sense of 44:19. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html
- Bible Hub summary: the separate kitchens keep holy meat out of common areas. It applies this to believers as "a royal priesthood". https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/46.htm

**vv. 21–22**
- Ellicott: each corner of the outer court had a place for boiling the meat of the peace offerings. They were quite large, 40 by 30 cubits, and seem to have been walled but open to the sky. The word for "joined" is uncertain, but probably means "enclosed." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm

**v. 23**
- Ellicott: tables of masonry ran around the walls, with boiling places underneath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown (JFB): the boiling places were built into the lowest part of the walls. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eze/Eze_046.cfm

**v. 24**
- Ellicott: the "ministers of the house" are not priests but temple servants, usually Levites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/46.htm
- Pulpit Commentary agrees they are Levites, who boil the sacrifice of the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-46.html

---

**Gaps (left out because I couldn't find them):**
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** Haydock's Catholic commentary has a chapter 46 page on StudyLight, but I couldn't read what it says. I found nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Modern scholarship:** nothing from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org.
- **Popular modern teaching:** nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
- **Named Methodist, Lutheran or Pentecostal sources:** none specific to this chapter.
